pedagogy.summary: Year 3 (age 7–8) extends money problems to pounds AND pence together: totalling two or three priced items and giving change from a whole amount such as £5 or £10, and recording with £ and p notation (e.g. £3.47). The efficient route to change from a note is the counting-on / finding-the-difference strategy, not written column subtraction across zeros. The central hazard is that £.p looks like two separate whole numbers: pupils must exchange 100p for £1 and treat the amount as one quantity. (Note: the statutory Y3 guidance records £ and p separately and defers formal decimal notation to Y4; this topic's evidence uses the £3.47 form, so teach the notation carefully alongside the pence-and-pounds meaning.)
bestPractices: Find change from £5/£10 by counting UP from the total spent to the note (e.g. spent £4.45 → +5p to £4.50 → +50p to £5.00; change 55p), shown on an empty number line — avoids error-prone column subtraction across zeros.
Establish 100p = £1 concretely and insist that £ and p are one quantity, not two whole numbers; exchange 100 pennies for a £1 coin so the equivalence is enacted.
Use the part–whole structure for multi-item change: total the items first (the parts), then the note is the whole and change is the missing part.
Model and contrast correct vs incorrect notation explicitly (£3.47, not £347, 3.47p or £3.47p); have pupils see, say and record amounts in more than one way.
Encourage estimation before calculating (≈£4.50 spent, so change is small) so unreasonable answers are caught, and read amounts in a place-value-honest way rather than as two separate numbers.
keyRepresentations: Empty number line for counting-on change from a note
Part–whole (bar) model: note = total cost + change
Place-value columns (£ | tenths/10p | hundredths/1p) shown aligned by the decimal point
commonMisconceptions: 'String-length thinking' — treats £ and p as two separate whole numbers (adds the pence column past 100 without exchanging, or writes £3.7 for £3 and 70p).
Notation errors — omits the decimal point, mixes units (£3.47p), or writes pence as if pounds.
Attempts change from £10 by column subtraction and makes 'take smaller from larger' / subtract-across-zeros errors instead of counting up.
'Most coins = most money' persists, and reading '£2.47' as 'two point forty-seven' reinforces the two-separate-numbers error.

learn.summary: Year 3 learners (age 7–8) total two or three items priced in pounds and pence, give change from a £5 or £10 note, and record amounts correctly (e.g. £3.47). The reliable route to change from a note is counting UP from the total spent to the note (finding the difference), not column subtraction across zeros. The central hazard is treating £.p as two separate whole numbers ('string-length thinking'); learners must exchange 100p for £1 and treat each amount as one quantity. Note: the National Curriculum's non-statutory notes and guidance for Year 3 say pupils record £ and p separately, and formal decimal recording of money is introduced in Year 4, so teach the £3.47 form carefully alongside its pence-and-pounds meaning.

activities.title: Shop till: total, pay, and count change up
feedback: If pence are added past 100 without exchanging (e.g. £2.60 + £1.85 written as £3.145 or £3.45), stop and build the pence physically, exchange 100p for a £1 coin, then re-read the total as a single quantity (the correct total is £4.45).

If change is reached by column subtraction from £5.00/£10.00 and digits are taken the wrong way across the zeros (e.g. 00 − 47 giving £1.47 or £2.53), redirect to counting UP from the total to the note on a number line.
Check any change by counting it back onto the total: does it rebuild £5.00? If not, the jumps were wrong.

OPTIONAL interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete: a total bar that sums items as they are added; a number line that draws each counting-on jump; a coin tray whose 100p visibly animates into one £1 coin. These are illustrative, not required — coins, a paper number line and spoken rehearsal achieve the same purposes.
activities.rationale: Counting up / finding the difference from the total to the note is an efficient change strategy that avoids subtract-across-zeros errors, and enacting 100p = £1 confronts the 'two separate whole numbers' misconception by making the exchange visible.
sourceClaims: Change is efficiently found by counting up / finding the difference from the total to the note (shopkeeper's method), avoiding column subtraction across zeros; many children count up more easily than they count back.

Children commonly treat pounds and pence (whole-number and decimal places) as two separate whole numbers rather than one decimal quantity ('string-length thinking'), partly because of whole-number language such as 'three pounds and seventy-six pence'; standard decimal vocal reading ('two point five four pounds') is recommended to counter this.

Year 3 pupils should add and subtract amounts of money to give change, using both £ and p in practical contexts; non-statutory guidance says they record pounds and pence separately and that decimal recording of money is introduced formally in Year 4.
learnerActions: Choose two or three priced items (e.g. a £2.60 car and a £1.85 book) and total them, building the total step by step (£2.60 + £1.85 = £4.45).
Pay with a £5 note and work out the change by counting UP from the total to the note, drawing each jump on an empty number line: £4.45 → +5p → £4.50 → +50p → £5.00, so change is 55p.
Collect the change as actual coins into a tray; when the pennies/pence in the tray reach 100p, physically exchange them for a single £1 coin and re-read the amount as one quantity.
Repeat for a single £3.47 item paid with a £5 note: count up £3.47 → £3.50 → £4.00 → £5.00 = £1.53.

Record the change in £ and p notation (e.g. £0.55, 55p), then say the amount in a place-value-honest way suitable for Year 3 (e.g. 'fifty-five pence'); avoid reading the pence as a compound whole number joined to the pounds (e.g. 'three point forty-seven' for £3.47). Reading the digits separately ('nought point five five') is also acceptable and is the decimal reading the cited research recommends.
activities.intendedInsight: Change from a note is a short counting-on jump from the total to the note, and an amount in pounds and pence is ONE quantity because 100p exchanges for £1.

activities.title: Record it right: correct versus incorrect money notation
feedback: If a learner writes £347 for £3.47, ask how many whole pounds that would be and compare with the coins in the tray.
If a learner writes £0.55p (£ and p together) or 55p inside pounds as £55, show the correct form next to it and ask which matches the coins.

Reinforce place-value-honest readings ('fifty-five pence', 'three pounds forty-seven pence') and reject only the compound-whole reading of the pence, such as 'three point forty-seven', which treats the pence like a separate whole number. Reading the digits separately ('three point four seven') is not an error and is the reading the cited research recommends.
activities.rationale: Notation and place-value errors (omitted decimal point, mixed units) are specific and nameable, and contrasting correct with incorrect forms at the moment of writing targets them directly.
sourceClaims: £ and p should not be written together (e.g. not £1.00p); pupils commonly record money incorrectly by omitting the decimal point or mixing units.

Children commonly treat pounds and pence (whole-number and decimal places) as two separate whole numbers rather than one decimal quantity ('string-length thinking'), partly because of whole-number language such as 'three pounds and seventy-six pence'; standard decimal vocal reading ('two point five four pounds') is recommended to counter this.
learnerActions: For a given amount of coins in a tray, write the amount in £ and p and check it against the coins.
Compare correct and incorrect recordings side by side (e.g. £0.55 vs £0.55p vs £55) and decide which one matches the coins, explaining how you know.
Record the same amount in more than one correct way where sensible (e.g. 55p and £0.55) and explain they are equal.
Practise see–say–record: see the coins, say the amount place-value-honestly, then write it without ever joining £ and p (never £3.47p).
activities.intendedInsight: Money notation carries meaning: the decimal point separates pounds from pence, £ and p are never written together, and the written amount must match the value of the coins.

activities.title: Estimate first, then check for sense
feedback: If an answer is wildly off (e.g. a change of £4.53 from £5 after spending £4.45, when only about 55p is expected), prompt the estimate check: does this match 'the change should be small'?
If the counting-back check does not rebuild the note, the jumps or columns were wrong — redo by counting up.
activities.rationale: Pupils rarely estimate first and so lack a sense of a sensible answer; building in estimation and a counting-back check gives a self-correction routine.
sourceClaims: Pupils make take-smaller-from-larger and subtract-across-zeros errors (e.g. in £10.00 − amount) reflecting weak exchange/place value, and rarely estimate first so lack a sense of a sensible answer.

Change is efficiently found by counting up / finding the difference from the total to the note (shopkeeper's method), avoiding column subtraction across zeros; many children count up more easily than they count back.
learnerActions: Before calculating change, estimate: 'I spent about £4.50, so the change should be small.'
After finding change, compare it with the estimate and say whether the answer is reasonable.
Verify change by counting it back onto the total to rebuild the note.
When paying with a £10 note instead of £5, predict how the change will differ and decide whether counting up or column subtraction would be easier.
activities.intendedInsight: Estimating before calculating catches unreasonable answers, and change from a note can always be checked by rebuilding the note.

activities.title: Quick checks on notation and reasonableness
feedback: For a wrong choice, point back to the coins or value the amount represents and ask which written form matches it.
Note: selecting a correct form checks notation and reasonableness but does not show the learner can carry out the counting-on process — pair it with the hands-on till activity.
activities.rationale: Short recognition checks are well suited to the crisply testable notation misconception and to reasonableness, as a companion to hands-on calculation rather than a replacement; recognition alone does not elicit the production of the counting-on method.
sourceClaims: £ and p should not be written together (e.g. not £1.00p); pupils commonly record money incorrectly by omitting the decimal point or mixing units.
learnerActions: Fill in the blank to record a shown amount in correct £ and p notation.
Choose which of several written forms correctly records a given amount (e.g. £3.47 among £347 and £3.47p, with the incorrect forms clearly present only as non-examples to be rejected).
Choose or state the correct change for a simple purchase from a note.
Put a set of money amounts in order from least to most to practise treating each as one quantity.
activities.intendedInsight: Correct notation and reasonable amounts can be recognised and chosen reliably once the single-quantity meaning is understood.

activities.title: Shopkeeper role-play to narrate the method (optional support)
feedback: Use this to rehearse and explain reasoning; it narrates the method but does not by itself give calculation practice with feedback, so follow it with actual totalling, change-finding and recording.
activities.rationale: Talking through the shopkeeper's counting-on method may support articulation of the strategy, but giving change is procedural and needs practice with feedback, which narration alone does not supply; the articulation benefit is a proposed, untested affordance.
learnerActions: Take the role of shopkeeper and, out loud, talk a 'customer' through giving change: name the total, then count up from the total to the note coin by coin.
Explain aloud why 100p becomes £1 while handing over the change.
activities.intendedInsight: Verbalising the counting-on method and the 100p→£1 exchange may help a learner articulate and consolidate the procedure.

constraints: Treat each money amount as ONE quantity: insist on exchanging 100p for £1, never carrying pence past 99 without exchanging and never writing three digits after the point.

Teach change from a £5/£10 note primarily by counting UP (finding the difference) on a number line; reserve column subtraction for cases without the across-zeros trap and only when done correctly with exchange.
Never present an incorrect money form (£347, £3.47p, £0.55p, pence written as pounds) as a correct option in a learner task; use such forms only as clearly labelled non-examples to be rejected.

Read amounts place-value-honestly for Year 3 ('three pounds and forty-seven pence', 'fifty-five pence'); the pitfall to avoid is reading the pence as a compound whole number joined to the pounds ('three point forty-seven'). Digit-by-digit decimal reading ('three point four seven') is acceptable and is the reading the cited research recommends.
Recognition/selection checks confirm notation and reasonableness but do not elicit the independent counting-on calculation; pair them with hands-on totalling, change-finding and recording.

The National Curriculum's non-statutory Year 3 notes and guidance say pupils record pounds and pence separately, with formal decimal recording of money introduced in Year 4; introduce the £3.47 form deliberately alongside its meaning, and expect some learners to still record pounds and pence separately.

Illustrative interactions (total bar, number-line jumps, 100p→£1 animation, coin tray) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete and must not be treated as the only valid medium; coins, paper number lines and spoken rehearsal achieve the same purposes.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source worked example £5.00 − £3.47 = £1.53 is arithmetically correct (count up: £3.47→£3.50 is 3p, →£4.00 is 50p, →£5.00 is £1, total £1.53); retained as stated. £2.60 + £1.85 = £4.45 is also correct.
The misconception examples '£3.145/£3.45', '£2.53' and '£1.47' are deliberately WRONG forms shown only as error patterns, never as correct answers.

Reading guidance: the original candidate banned 'point five five', but the Cambridge source actually recommends digit-by-digit decimal reading ('two point five four pounds') to counter string-length thinking; only reading the pence as a compound whole number ('three point forty-seven') reinforces the two-separate-numbers error. The Year-3-appropriate reading remains 'fifty-five pence'/'three pounds and forty-seven pence', with digit-by-digit decimal reading flagged as acceptable rather than wrong. The Cambridge source also flags compound whole-number language as partly causing the misconception, so the exact convention is a teacher judgement.

The shopkeeper role-play activity had its sourceClaims set to [] because the attached counting-up claim supports only the method content, not the untested principle that verbalisation/role-play aids consolidation; the benefit is stated as proposed/may.

One cited source (NCETM, 'Misconceptions with the Key Objectives') is marked verified:false in the row; its claim about take-smaller-from-larger, subtract-across-zeros and lack of estimation is used to inform feedback but should be treated with that lower confidence.

The row notes a genuine tension: evidence materials use the £3.47 decimal form while statutory Y3 guidance records pounds and pence separately and defers decimals to Y4; teachers should resolve this against their curriculum sequence.

probeDeeper: 'Read that amount to me — is £3.47 one number or two? What does the 4 mean, and the 7?'
'Check your change by counting it back onto £4.45 — does it rebuild £5?'
'You have £0.55 and £55 written down — which one matches the coins, and how do you know?'
'What if you'd paid with a £10 note instead of £5 — how would the change change, and would column subtraction or counting up be easier?'
assess.correctAnswer: Totals £2.60 + £1.85 = £4.45; finds change by counting up £4.45 → £4.50 → £5.00 = 55p (or column subtraction done correctly with exchange), and records it as £0.55 / 55p in consistent notation. For the game: £5.00 − £3.47 = £1.53, again best reached by counting on. Treats each amount as one quantity, exchanging 100p for £1 where needed.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'String-length thinking' — treats £ and p as two separate whole numbers: adds the pence beyond 100 without exchanging (£2.60 + £1.85 → £3.145 or £3.45), or subtracts pounds and pence columns independently.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Enact 100p = £1 with coins: build up the pence, physically exchange ten 10p (or 100 pennies) for a £1 coin, and re-read the amount as one quantity. Say amounts place-value-honestly, not as two separate numbers.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Column work where the pence exceed 99 without carrying a pound, or a total/answer with three digits after the point, or pence treated as their own number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Notation error — omits the decimal point or mixes units: records the change as £347, £55, 55p written inside pounds, or £0.55p (£ and p together).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show correct and incorrect side by side (£0.55 vs £0.55p vs £55) and ask which matches the coins in the tray; rehearse see–say–record and never writing £ and p together.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The written amount doesn't match its value, or combines £ and p symbols, or drops/misplaces the decimal point.

errorPatterns.pattern: Column-subtracts change from a whole note and makes take-smaller-from-larger / subtract-across-zeros errors (£5.00 − £3.47 treated as 00 − 47 = 47, giving £1.47 or £2.53) instead of counting up.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Redirect to the efficient strategy: find change from a note by counting UP from the total to the note on a number line, and reserve column methods for cases without the zeros trap.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A written vertical subtraction from £5.00/£10.00 with digits taken the wrong way across the zeros; an answer that doesn't survive a counting-back check.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot total £.p or exchange 100p→£1; treats pounds and pence as separate whole numbers and records inconsistent notation.
responseLevels.full: Totals two or three £.p items, finds change from £5/£10 by counting up, records £-notation correctly and consistently, treats each amount as a single quantity (exchanging 100p→£1), and transfers to a new price or note.
responseLevels.partial: Totals and gives change for a friendly case, but stumbles on change from a whole £5/£10 (column-across-zeros error) or records £.p inconsistently; can list the amounts but not treat them as one quantity throughout.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a small shop of priced items and real/realistic coins and notes. Say: 'Buy the £2.60 car and the £1.85 book. Pay with this £5 note, work out the change, and write down the change using £ and p.' Then: 'Now buy just the £3.47 game and pay with a £5 note — what's the change?' Watch the method and the notation, not only the final number.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with a single-quantity understanding of £.p counts up (or exchanges cleanly) and records £0.55 correctly; a child holding 'two separate whole numbers' adds/subtracts the pounds and pence columns independently (yielding e.g. £3.150, or £2.53 by taking 47 from 00), or writes £347/£0.55p. The counting-on change and the notation each expose a different, nameable error.
